title: Debugging with distributed traces: waterfall shapes, context propagation & sampling
description: A distributed trace shows one request's path through every service it touched. Once you learn to read its shape, you can often spot the bug before you open a single log. This quiz shows you span waterfalls and asks what went wrong: N+1 staircases, stragglers, retry storms, clock skew, and broken handoffs. The last questions cover sampling, which decides whether the trace you need gets kept at all.

questions.title: In a trace waterfall, Span B is drawn indented inside Span A and starts after A begins. What does that mean?

options.text: B is a child of A. A called whatever B represents and is still running while it waits for B.
B happened after A finished. The indentation just marks the second event.
B belongs to a different trace that got merged into this view.
B is a retry of A that ran only because A failed.

questions.explanation: Nesting shows who called whom. When a span sits indented inside another, the outer operation called the inner one and stays open until the inner one returns. Two spans at the same depth that don't overlap are siblings that ran one after the other. Read a waterfall as a call graph laid out on a timeline, and the order of events comes with it.

questions.title: A trace's root span lasts 800 ms. Its two direct children last 150 ms and 200 ms. What can you say about the other 450 ms?

options.text: The trace doesn't explain it. It's the root span's own work, or waiting with no child span around it, before, after, or between the children.
It's a measurement bug. A root span's duration should equal the sum of its children.
It's network latency from the root span's own instrumentation overhead.
The tracer rounded the two children up to fill the parent's box.

questions.explanation: A parent span's duration is the wall-clock time from its start to its end. Nothing forces it to match the sum of its children. The missing 450 ms could be local CPU work with no span around it, a gap between the two calls, or setup and cleanup before and after the calls. A wide span with unexplained time is a hint to add instrumentation. It isn't a bug in the tracer.

questions.title: A parent span is much wider than its only child, with large stretches of unexplained time on both sides. What does that usually mean?
questions.description: In the waterfall below, one parent span holds a single, much shorter child.

images.alt: A wide parent span labeled checkout.process, with a much shorter child span labeled payment.charge nested near its middle, leaving large gaps of unexplained time before and after the child

options.text: Local CPU work in the parent, or a call to something nobody instrumented, like a library or a subprocess. The trace alone can't tell you which.
The child span's clock is wrong, so its timestamps don't line up with the parent's.
The parent was sampled and the child wasn't, so the child's duration is under-reported.
The OS suspended the process during the gaps, and tracers always report that exactly.

questions.explanation: A trace can't see time that no span covers. The gap could be real CPU work such as parsing, serialization, or a tight loop. It could also be a call nobody wrapped in a span, like a native library, a child process, or a client SDK without tracing support. The waterfall shows roughly where time went missing, but not why. Wrap the suspect code in a span and check the next trace instead of guessing from the shape.

questions.title: Two sibling spans share a parent, and there's a gap between them with nothing else in the trace. What could cause the gap?
questions.description: Both spans below are children of `svc-a.request`. They run one after the other with empty time between them.

images.alt: Two sibling spans, step1 and step2, both children of svc-a.request, with an empty gap of time between the end of step1 and the start of step2

options.text: Time between the two calls that no span recorded. Waiting on a queue, a GC pause, and lock contention are common causes.
It's always network latency between two remote calls.
step2 was sampled out and then back in, and the viewer draws that as a gap.
The tracer buffers spans before exporting them, and the gap is that export delay.

questions.explanation: A gap between siblings is real elapsed time that nothing recorded. Anything that stalls the thread without making a traced call can cause it, such as waiting for a queue or thread pool, a garbage collection pause, waiting on a lock, or CPU scheduling delay under load. Network latency is unlikely, because a remote call would usually show up as its own span. The fix is the same as for an oversized span. Add events or child spans around the suspect step so the next trace explains the gap.

questions.title: Why might a trace waterfall and a service's log timestamps disagree about when something happened?

options.text: Logs are often written and flushed asynchronously, stamped by the writing process's clock. The tracer records span timestamps the moment each operation starts and ends.
Traces use atomic clocks, so they're always more accurate.
Logs can't carry timestamps, so there's nothing to compare.
They always match once you round to the nearest second.

questions.explanation: Log lines are often batched and flushed after the event they describe, stamped by whatever clock the writing process has, and sometimes reordered by async handlers. A trace records each span's start and end as the operation happens, and links spans by parent and child instead of by line order. That keeps a trace closer to the real order of events. Clocks on different machines cause their own problems, which a later question covers.

questions.title: What's the difference between a span attribute and a span event?

options.text: An attribute is a key-value fact about the whole span, like `http.status_code`. An event is a timestamped moment inside the span, like a cache miss at 120 ms.
Attributes exist only on the root span, and events only on child spans.
Events are attributes that were renamed for compatibility with older tracing libraries.
An attribute records something that happened once. An event holds several values that change over the span's lifetime.

questions.explanation: Attributes describe the span as a whole and have no timestamp of their own. Events mark something that happened at one instant during the span, such as a caught exception, a retry, or a cache miss, without the cost of a new span. Both are standard OpenTelemetry terms. The difference matters when you read a waterfall, because events often sit in a list you have to click open instead of on the timeline.

questions.title: A parent span holds many identical child spans of the same length, running one after another and filling most of the parent. What does that usually mean?
questions.description: Below, `GET /orders` has eight near-identical `db.query` spans back to back.

images.alt: A parent span labeled GET /orders, with eight identical db.query child spans of the same width running one after another beneath it, like a staircase

options.text: An N+1 query. The code loops over a list and runs one query per item instead of one query for the whole batch.
One slow query that the tracer reported as many separate spans by mistake.
A retry storm, where a client keeps resending the same request after errors.
A fan-out that split independent work up to run in parallel.

questions.explanation: Many spans with the same name and about the same duration, packed end to end, is the classic N+1 shape. The code loops over a collection and runs one query per item. Batch the query, or use a data loader that combines per-item requests, and the staircase becomes one wider span. Two lookalikes to rule out: a retry storm has growing gaps between repeats, and a fan-out runs its calls at the same time instead of in sequence.

questions.title: Two traces of the same endpoint and code path look very different. One has a staircase of database queries, the other a single short span. What's the most likely reason?
questions.description: Both waterfalls below use the same time scale.

images.alt: Two waterfalls on the same time scale: trace A shows handle-request with a staircase of six db.query spans; trace B shows handle-request with a single short cache.get span
images.caption: Both traces hit the same endpoint and the same code.

options.text: Trace A missed the cache, so the N+1 loop hit the database. Trace B hit the cache, and one fast lookup replaced all those queries.
The endpoint has two different implementations, and the traces are unrelated.
Trace B was sampled at a lower rate, so most of its spans were dropped.
The database was down during trace A, so every query in the loop retried.

questions.explanation: A warm cache can hide an N+1 loop. When the cache answers the whole loop in one call, the staircase shrinks to a single span, as in trace B. If you only look at traces from normal warm traffic, you can miss the problem entirely. It shows up on a cold cache, after an eviction, or on the first request after a deploy, which is when it hurts most.

questions.title: The three child spans below don't depend on each other, and none needs another's output. Yet the trace shows them running one after another. What's going on?
questions.description: The parent is `GET /dashboard`; the three children are `get-user`, `get-orders`, and `get-recommendations`.

images.alt: A parent span GET /dashboard with three independent child spans, get-user, get-orders, and get-recommendations, running one after another with no overlap
The same three calls shown before and after the fix: serial, ending at 450 ms, and parallel, ending at 200 ms
images.caption: After the fix, the three calls overlap and the parent shrinks to the slowest one.

options.text: The code `await`s each call before starting the next, so three calls that could run together run in sequence.
The three services share a physical server, so they can't run at the same time.
The tracer always draws sibling spans one after another for readability, even if they overlapped.
Context propagation allows only one outgoing call per parent span, so the others had to wait.

questions.explanation: An `await` stops the next line from starting, whether or not that line needs the result. Three independent calls awaited one by one cost the sum of their durations. Start them together with `Promise.all` or structured concurrency, then await them as a group, and they cost only as much as the slowest one. This is one of the most common shapes in a waterfall and one of the easiest to fix, because the change stays inside one service.

questions.title: You fix the problem above by starting all three calls before awaiting any of them. What should the parent's duration be closest to now?

options.text: The duration of the slowest child call, since the three now run at the same time.
The sum of the three original child durations, since the same work still happens.
Close to zero, since concurrent calls don't count toward the parent's duration.
Exactly the average of the three original child durations.

questions.explanation: When independent calls run at the same time, the wait is as long as the slowest call. The total work stays the same, but the calls stop waiting on each other. The same rule applies to fan-out elsewhere in this quiz: a parent that waits on concurrent children takes as long as its longest child.

questions.title: A service fans out to five independent calls. Four return in about 50 ms and one takes 310 ms. Why is the parent span 310 ms wide?
questions.description: All five children below start at the same time as direct children of `aggregate`.

images.alt: A parent span aggregate with five child spans starting at the same time; four are short and similar in length, one is much longer and highlighted in a different color

options.text: The parent waits for every child before it responds, so the slowest child sets its duration.
The parent's clock started late, so it only looks like it ends after the slow child.
The four fast children were sampled out, and they really took much longer.
The 310 ms child retried three times, and the parent shows only the last attempt.

questions.explanation: When a span fans out to independent children and waits for all of them, its duration equals the slowest child's. That's the straggler problem. One slow dependency, even one that's usually fast, can decide how long the whole request takes. It's why aggregation endpoints often have worse tail latency than any service they call. A later question works out how much a wide fan-out makes this worse.

questions.title: A parent span fans out to many independent children and waits for all of them. Which statements are true?

options.text: The parent's p99 latency depends on the children's slow tails more than on their typical latency.
All else equal, adding more independent children can only make the parent's tail latency worse.
If every child has a p99 of 100 ms, the parent's p99 is also 100 ms.
One very slow child among many fast ones can dominate the parent's time, even if that child is rarely slow.

questions.explanation: A parent that waits for all its children takes as long as whichever child is slowest on that request. Each extra child is another chance that one of them is slow, and a later question asks you to run those numbers. So the parent is slower than its typical child. A dependency that is rarely slow still sets the duration of the requests where it is the straggler, which makes the parent's p99 worse than any single child's.

questions.title: The waterfall shows the same child span repeated several times, with a longer gap before each repeat. What does this usually mean?
questions.description: The parent is `publish-event`; the repeated child is `call-webhook`.

images.alt: A parent span publish-event with the same call-webhook child span repeated four times, with the gap before each successive repeat growing larger than the last

options.text: A retry loop with backoff. Each attempt fails or times out, and the growing gaps are the wait before the next retry.
A batch job that spaces out identical work on purpose to avoid overloading a downstream service.
Clock skew that makes one call look like it repeats in the waterfall.
The tracer deduplicated a span incorrectly and drew it several times.

questions.explanation: The same child span repeating with gaps that grow, often doubling each time, is a retry loop with backoff. The call keeps failing or timing out, and each gap is a deliberate delay before the next attempt. Work that is spaced out on purpose usually doesn't repeat one operation under one parent with doubling delays. Also check how much of the parent's latency budget the retries used up. That's worth flagging even when the last attempt succeeds.

questions.title: A child span seems to start 30 ms before its parent. The child's service is healthy, and its logs show it started only after it received the request. What's the most likely explanation?
questions.description: Both spans below are on the same timeline, with the parent's start time marked.

images.alt: Two spans on a shared timeline: gateway.request and svc-b.handle, where svc-b.handle's bar begins to the left of a marked line showing where gateway.request begins

options.text: Clock skew. Different machines timestamped the two spans, and their clocks differ slightly. The timeline looks wrong, but nothing happened out of order.
The trace collector has a bug that makes the timeline run backward.
The child span belongs to a request that hadn't been sent yet.
Context propagation failed, so the child got attached to a random parent.

questions.explanation: Each span gets its timestamps from the clock of the machine that created it. Keeping clocks in sync is hard because of NTP drift, VM clock jumps, and container scheduling delays, so a small negative overlap at a service boundary is common and harmless. A large or consistent skew is an infrastructure problem worth chasing, but 30 ms is noise.

questions.title: You expect a trace to continue from `checkout-api` into `shipping-service`. Instead, the trace ends at `checkout-api`, and a separate trace starts in `shipping-service` at about the same moment. What's the most likely cause?

images.alt: Two separate span trees drawn side by side with no connecting edge: checkout-api.request with its child inventory-service.call on the left, and shipping-service.request with its child shipping-service.call on the right

Two diagrams of a traceparent header crossing a service boundary: one where the header is forwarded and both services share a trace id, and one where the header is dropped and the second service mints a new trace id

options.text: Context propagation is broken at that boundary. The `traceparent` header (or equivalent) isn't forwarded, so `shipping-service` starts a new trace.
The two services use different sample rates, which makes one trace look shorter.
`shipping-service` is slower than `checkout-api`, so the viewer draws its span separately.
The two span trees come from unrelated requests that happen to overlap in time.

questions.explanation: Distributed tracing works only if every network hop forwards the trace context, usually in a `traceparent` header that carries the trace id and parent span id. If a proxy strips headers, a message broker drops them, or a client SDK was never set up for tracing, the next service has no context to continue from. It creates a new trace id and becomes its own root. Nothing throws an error. One trace just stops, and an unrelated-looking one starts at almost the same moment.

questions.title: Which of these, seen in a tracing system, point to broken context propagation somewhere in the request path?

options.text: A trace that stops at a service boundary, with no child span for a call you know the code makes.
A second root span with a different trace id, starting at about the moment the missing call should have happened.
A message-queue consumer whose spans never show up under the producer's trace, even though the producer waits for the message to be processed.
A child span that is indented under its parent and starts slightly after the parent begins.

questions.explanation: The first three options are the usual signs: a trace that stops early, a new root trace that appears when the missing call should have happened, and queue or async hops that never link back to the producer. Queues are a common blind spot, because nothing carries context across them automatically the way a header does on an HTTP call. The last option is normal nesting, which is what a correctly propagated call looks like.

questions.title: A span named `resize-image` takes 480 ms of a 500 ms parent, and a developer concludes that resizing is slow. In the code, the span wraps both the resize and a network upload of the result. What does this teach about span durations?
questions.description: The waterfall below shows only what the trace can see: one child span filling almost the whole parent.

images.alt: A parent span process-image with a single child span, resize-image, that fills nearly the entire width of the parent

options.text: A span's duration tells you how long the wrapped code ran, not what it was doing. Wrap too much and the name points at the wrong operation.
The duration always matches exactly the operation the span is named after, so the upload must be the fast part.
This can't happen, because tracers automatically split a wrapped function into one span per line of code.
Rename the span to `resize-image-and-upload` and stop investigating.

questions.explanation: The span's timing is correct. It reports exactly how long the wrapped code took. The problem is that it wraps more work than its name says, so the name points at the wrong operation. Narrow the span, or add a child span for each real step, until the waterfall matches what the code does. Renaming it to `resize-image-and-upload` is more honest, but you still won't know which half took the 480 ms.

questions.title: The `http.request` span ends at 120 ms. A `send-email` span for the same request starts at 150 ms, drawn in its own row and connected by a link instead of nested inside. What does this usually mean?

images.alt: http.request ends, and afterward a separate span, send-email, appears in its own row, connected to http.request by a dashed link rather than being nested inside it

options.text: Work that continues after the response went out, such as a background or fire-and-forget task. It's linked because it isn't a normal child call within the request.
A bug where the tracer lost track of the real parent span.
The email went out before the response, and the diagram has the order wrong.
The request will time out, because the email span outlives the request span.

questions.explanation: Most tracers support span links for related work that doesn't block the caller. The usual case is background or queued work that a request starts and never awaits before sending the response. The linked span starts after the parent has finished, sits outside it, and its duration says nothing about how long the client waited. Those clues tell you the system kept working after the client already had its answer.

questions.title: Which of these would make you suspect a span is async handoff work, rather than blocking work the parent waited on?

options.text: The span starts after the span for the HTTP response has already ended.
The span joins the trace through a link instead of being nested as a child.
The span's duration has no effect on how long the client waited for its response.
The span is nested inside the request span and ends before the request span does.

questions.explanation: The first three are signs of async handoff: the work starts after the response is gone, it joins the trace by a link, and its duration never reaches the client. The last option is ordinary synchronous work, a child nested in its parent that finishes first. The client waited for that one.

questions.title: Six database query spans in one trace share a pattern: a long, equal wait before each query runs, then a short burst of real work. What does that equal wait suggest?

images.alt: Six db.query spans, each drawn as a dashed waiting segment of the same length followed by a short solid segment representing the query actually running
images.caption: The dashed portion is time spent waiting; the solid portion is the query itself.

options.text: Connection pool exhaustion. Each query waits for a free connection from a full pool before it can start, and everyone competing for the pool waits about the same time.
Each query does the same real work, so the wait must be a drawing artifact of the trace viewer.
Each query is retried a fixed number of times before it succeeds.
The database rate-limits every query by the same fixed delay.

questions.explanation: When many concurrent spans all start with the same wait, they're usually competing for a scarce resource such as database connections, worker threads, or a semaphore. The work itself isn't slow. A retry storm looks different, with growing gaps between repeats of one call, and so does an N+1 staircase, where queries run end to end. The usual fixes are a bigger pool, better connection reuse, or fewer queries per request. That last one may point back to an N+1 problem upstream.

questions.title: A team samples 1% of traces with head-based sampling. To keep every trace for one customer id, they add that filter to the sampler. Why does this often not work?

options.text: Head-based sampling decides at the root span whether to keep a trace, often before the customer id is known.
Head-based sampling only works with numeric attributes, and customer ids are usually strings.
1% is too low a sample rate for head-based sampling to work at all.
Head-based sampling always keeps 100% of traces, whatever the configuration.

questions.explanation: Head-based sampling decides keep or drop at the root, and every descendant span follows that decision. If the attribute you want to filter on appears later, for example after authentication or on a downstream span, it isn't there when the decision is made. To filter on attributes like that, use tail-based sampling, which waits for the whole trace before deciding.

questions.title: Tail-based sampling decides whether to keep a trace only after the trace has finished. What's its main cost?

images.alt: Two identical trace shapes, one with the sampling decision marked at the root before any children run, the other with the decision marked only after every child span has finished

options.text: Every span of every trace has to be buffered until the trace finishes. That takes memory and infrastructure, especially for long or high-volume traces.
Tail-based sampling can't keep slow or failing traces, only average ones.
Every service in the request path must sample at exactly the same percentage.
It works only for synchronous, single-service requests.

questions.explanation: Because tail-based sampling sees the outcome first, it can keep the traces you care about, the slow ones and the failing ones. The price is infrastructure. A collector holds every span of every in-progress trace until the trace finishes, then decides whether to keep it. That's a much heavier, stateful pipeline than head-based sampling's coin flip at the root.

questions.title: In an incident review, someone says 'we have no traces for the outage.' What's the most likely reason?

options.text: Head-based sampling kept only a small fixed percentage of traces, and the affected requests weren't in that random sample.
Tracing systems stop recording during outages as a built-in safety feature.
Traces are deleted automatically when an error status code is recorded.
The service used metrics instead of traces, so no traces could exist.

questions.explanation: With a low fixed head-sampling rate, the requests that mattered during the incident were no more likely to be kept than any others. At 1%, the bad traffic you need has a poor chance of surviving. Common fixes are raising the rate during risky periods, switching to tail-based sampling so errors and slow traces are kept on purpose, or keeping a way to force sampling for live debugging.

questions.title: You need to know how often an error code occurred across all traffic last week, by hour. Which kind of telemetry answers this directly?

options.text: Metrics. A counter or rate aggregated over time is what metrics are for, and you don't need to store or scan individual traces.
Traces. Pull every trace from the past week and count the ones with that error.
Logs. Parsing raw log lines from scratch beats a pre-aggregated counter.
Span events. Attach an event to every span and count them at query time.

questions.explanation: Each signal answers a different kind of question. Metrics answer how often and how much, cheaply and at high volume, because they're aggregated when written. Traces show where one request spent its time. Logs tell you in detail what happened in one case. You can count errors from traces or raw logs, but it's slow and wasteful compared with a counter built for the job.

questions.title: A user id is fine as a span attribute but dangerous as a metric label. Which of these explain why?

options.text: Metric systems usually create a new time series for every unique combination of label values, so a user id label can create an unbounded number of series.
Traces are stored and queried per request, so one more distinct attribute value doesn't multiply state elsewhere.
Tracing backends never index span attributes, so cardinality doesn't matter there.
Metric backends can slow down, get expensive, or silently drop data when label cardinality explodes.

questions.explanation: The difference is cardinality. Metrics keep one time series per unique combination of label values, so an unbounded label like a user id or a raw URL creates series without limit and can degrade or break the backend. Traces store each span on its own instead of rolling them into a fixed set of series, so one more distinct value costs very little. It isn't free, since many tracing backends index some attributes, but the cost grows far more slowly.

questions.title: Which of these questions are best answered by reading an individual trace, rather than metrics or logs?

options.text: "For this one slow request, which downstream call took the time?"
"For this kind of request, which services on the critical path does the time go to?"
"What is the 99th percentile latency for this endpoint over the last 24 hours?"
"What was the exact stack trace and error message when this specific request failed?"

questions.explanation: A trace shows how one request moved through every service it touched. That's what you need to find where its time went or which service sits on its critical path. A percentile over 24 hours of traffic is an aggregation, which is what metrics are for. The exact error message and stack trace for one failure belong in logs. A trace can link to them but doesn't store them.

questions.title: A parent span fans out to 5 independent calls. Each call has a 2% chance of being slow, meaning a 98% chance of finishing within its p99 threshold. What's the probability, in whole percent, that at least one of the 5 is slow?
questions.description: Use `P(at least one slow) = 1 - (0.98)^5`. Answer in whole percent, for example `25` for 25%.
questions.explanation: `1 - 0.98^5 ≈ 1 - 0.904 = 0.096`, or about 10%. Each dependency is reliable on its own, but a wide fan-out gives more chances for one of them to be slow on any given request. The parent waits for all five, so that one slow call sets its latency. That's why aggregation endpoints have worse tail latency than the services they call. The usual fixes are hedged requests, per-call timeouts with a fallback, or a narrower fan-out.

questions.title: A trace shows three independent calls made one after another: 120 ms, 260 ms, and 90 ms, for a parent of 470 ms. If they ran in parallel instead, about how many milliseconds would the parent save?
questions.description: Assume parallelizing adds no overhead, and the parallel duration equals the slowest call.
questions.explanation: In parallel, the parent takes as long as the slowest call, `260 ms`. In sequence it took the sum, `470 ms`. The saving is `470 - 260 = 210 ms`. Parallelizing turns a sum into a maximum. You save the most when the calls are similar in length. When one call already dominates, you save less, because that call still sets the minimum.

questions.title: A parent waits on 4 independent children that take 45 ms, 52 ms, 310 ms, and 60 ms. The parent does no work of its own. How long is the parent span, in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: A parent that waits for all its children takes as long as the slowest one, so this parent takes 310 ms. The three fast children don't change that. This is the straggler shape from earlier, as plain arithmetic.
